record.title: CICL reports improved first-file retrieval from decision-aware reranking on a small coding benchmark
record.summary: The v4 preprint presents the Counterfactual-Inspired Context Layer (CICL), which ranks candidate repository evidence by estimated effect on an agent’s next action and can compress selected context into typed memory cards. On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, the authors report that Qwen3.6-Plus reranking of BM25 top-50 candidates raises hit@1 from 0.58 to 0.78 and MRR@10 from 0.634 to 0.790. Top-10 recall is 0.714 versus 0.716, and the result measures file retrieval rather than patch success. The paper’s own terminology is counterfactual-inspired; it does not claim formal causal identification.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: CICL scores candidate context units by estimated decision-oriented utility and can pack selected evidence into typed memory cards under a token budget.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, Qwen3.6-Plus reranking of BM25 top-50 candidates reports hit@1 0.78 versus 0.58 and MRR@10 0.790 versus 0.634; R@10 is 0.714 versus 0.716.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED

evidence_gaps.description: The 50-instance retrieval results and associated judgments have not been independently reproduced.
The paper measures file retrieval rather than downstream patch success or end-to-end agent utility on the main real-code result.
The counterfactual-inspired score is not a formally identified causal effect, and LLM-judge annotations are not human gold labels.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated, decision-aware context reranking could help coding agents surface the right repository evidence earlier and pack it more efficiently. The reported gain is limited to file retrieval on 50 SWE-bench Verified instances, overall top-10 recall is unchanged, and no end-to-end patch success benefit is established.
limitations: All measurements are paper-reported; the research desk did not execute code or reproduce results.
The main real-code comparison is file retrieval on 50 SWE-bench Verified instances and does not measure patch success.
Top-10 recall is 0.714 versus 0.716 for BM25/HybridRAG despite higher hit@1 and MRR@10.
The paper states that counterfactual-inspired utility is not formal causal identification; structured model judgments are not human gold labels.
Synthetic rankings and compression diagnostics do not establish end-to-end deployment benefit.
brief.summary: The v4 preprint presents the Counterfactual-Inspired Context Layer (CICL), which ranks candidate repository evidence by estimated effect on an agent’s next action and can compress selected context into typed memory cards. On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, the authors report that Qwen3.6-Plus reranking of BM25 top-50 candidates raises hit@1 from 0.58 to 0.78 and MRR@10 from 0.634 to 0.790. Top-10 recall is 0.714 versus 0.716, and the result measures file retrieval rather than patch success. The paper’s own terminology is counterfactual-inspired; it does not claim formal causal identification.

technical.claimed_result: On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, Qwen3.6-Plus reranking BM25 top-50 candidates reports hit@1 0.78 vs 0.58 and MRR@10 0.790 vs 0.634; R@10 is 0.714 vs 0.716. A controlled synthetic v3 removal test reports context F1 falling from 0.245 to 0.000 when the top-utility unit is removed. In selected-then-compressed RepoBench-R mode, the abstract reports 44.93 fewer tokens per query while preserving selected evidence. These are author-reported results, and the 50-instance result is file retrieval rather than patch success.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v4 paper and linked abstract report the method, evaluation setup and metrics. the research desk did not run code, reproduce the benchmark, or verify downstream patch outcomes; results remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: CICL builds an instance context graph of files, symbols, memories, rules and failures; estimates decision-oriented utility for candidate units using structured judgments or rankers; and selects units under a token budget. Optional typed memory cards package a trigger, evidence, action hint, failure-if-ignored and scope. The paper describes the utility as counterfactual-inspired rather than formally causally identified.
technical.regime: SWE-bench Verified file-level retrieval on 50 instances, using Qwen3.6-Plus to rerank BM25 top-50 candidates; 2,500 judgments are reported parseable. Separate synthetic v1/v3 suites use 250 tasks each. RepoBench-R compression uses 100 tasks. A GPT-5.5 via Codex provider check covers only the first five SWE-bench instances.
technical.strongest_baseline: BM25/HybridRAG on the same 50-instance file-retrieval task: hit@1 0.58, MRR@10 0.634, and R@10 0.716 versus Qwen3.6-Plus CICL reranking at 0.78, 0.790 and 0.714. Stronger synthetic baselines remain competitive; on synthetic v3 VanillaRAG exceeds CICL F1.

brief.title: CICL reports improved first-file retrieval from decision-aware reranking on a small coding benchmark
brief.why_it_matters: Coding agents can receive many plausible repository files yet still miss the evidence that changes the next command or edit. CICL proposes measuring context by its estimated decision utility, with a small real-code retrieval result and controlled synthetic diagnostics. The narrow file-level gain is worth tracking, but it does not establish improved software repair, broader agent performance, or a causal effect in deployment.
